questions.title: Why does the partition function Z(x) cancel when deriving the DPO preference probability?
questions.question_body: In the DPO paper, they start from the optimal policy form for the KL-constrained objective, namely \(\pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)\). Rearranging gives \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x)\), where \(Z(x)\) is the partition function. Plugging this into the Bradley–Terry model \(p(y_1\succ y_2\mid x)=\sigma(r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2))\) yields the DPO objective where \(Z(x)\) cancels. I understand that the difference \(r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)\) removes any \(f(x)\)-type additive terms, but I am confused about the precise conditions: does the cancellation rely only on the two responses sharing the same prompt \(x\)? Do variable-length completions or EOS handling make \(Z(x)\) implicitly depend on length in a way that could fail to cancel? Finally, are there support assumptions (e.g., \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)>0\) for all logged \(y\)) needed so that the log-ratios are well-defined?

questions.title: How is the closed-form optimal policy for the KL-constrained objective derived in the DPO paper?
questions.question_body: The paper states that the solution to maximizing \(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[r(x,y)]-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi(\cdot\mid x)\Vert\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)]\) has the Boltzmann form \(\pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)\). Could someone walk through the derivation step by step for the discrete sequence case? In particular: (1) how is the Lagrangian set up for the constraint that \(\sum_y \pi(y\mid x)=1\), (2) how does one take functional derivatives to obtain the exponential form, and (3) is the KL the sequence-level KL or a per-token KL, and does that choice matter for the derivation?

questions.title: In DPO, is log \(\pi(y\mid x)\) computed over entire sequences or per-token, and how is length bias handled?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss uses terms like \(\log\tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}\). For an autoregressive LM, this sequence probability is a product over tokens, so the log-probability is a sum over time steps. Does the implementation use the total sequence log-probability or a length-normalized average (e.g., per-token)? If it is the total, how does DPO avoid a bias toward shorter responses, since longer sequences accumulate more negative log-probability? If it is normalized, where is that stated and how is EOS handled in the log-prob calculation?

questions.title: What exactly does the \(\beta\) hyperparameter control in DPO, and how should I pick it to target a KL?
questions.question_body: The paper describes \(\beta\) as controlling the strength of the KL constraint via the mapping \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}+\beta\log Z(x)\), and it appears in the DPO loss inside the log-ratio. Practically, how does \(\beta\) affect (1) the achieved KL \(\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi\Vert\pi_{\text{ref}}]\), (2) the gradient magnitudes, and (3) the trade-off between exploiting preferences and staying close to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? Is there a monotonic relationship between \(\beta\) and the realized KL in practice, so that we can tune \(\beta\) to hit a target KL the way PPO targets a KL?

questions.title: Why does the DPO gradient include a sigmoid weighting term, and what breaks if we omit it (i.e., use naive unlikelihood)?
questions.question_body: The gradient sketch shows a weight of \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\) multiplying the difference of score functions \(\nabla_\theta\log\pi(y_w\mid x)-\nabla_\theta\log\pi(y_l\mid x)\). Intuitively this upweights pairs the model currently misorders. What precisely goes wrong if we drop the sigmoid weight and simply push up \(\log\pi(y_w\mid x)\) and push down \(\log\pi(y_l\mid x)\) (unlikelihood)? Can someone give a simple example or argument showing how the unweighted objective encourages degeneration (e.g., collapsing to short answers or suppressing diversity) that the DPO weighting avoids?

questions.title: Is DPO truly equivalent to PPO-based RLHF on the same Bradley–Terry objective, or only in the limit of infinite data?
questions.question_body: The paper claims DPO "implicitly optimizes the same objective as existing RLHF algorithms (reward maximization with a KL-divergence constraint)." However, DPO trains on a fixed offline set of pairs, while PPO learns on-policy with respect to the evolving \(\pi_\theta\). Under what conditions do the solutions of DPO and PPO coincide? Is the equivalence exact only at the population level (infinite preference data drawn from the optimal policy’s preference distribution), or does it hold for finite datasets? How does off-distribution bias from the fixed dataset affect the equivalence?

questions.title: How does DPO handle reference-policy mismatch when preference data were generated by a different model?
questions.question_body: In practice, the paper suggests initializing \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) by maximizing the likelihood of the preferred responses \(y_w\) if the original SFT model used to collect pairs is unavailable. Why train \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) only on \(y_w\) and not also on \(y_l\)? Does this choice introduce a bias in the implicit reward \(\hat r_\theta=\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\) that could inflate the reward scale? Are there diagnostics to tell if this reference-policy retrofit sufficiently mitigates distribution shift, or should we also include negatives or regularize toward a base LM?

questions.title: What assumptions are needed for the theorem that any reward class can be written as \(\beta\log \pi/\pi_{\text{ref}}\)?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 asserts that, under mild assumptions, every reward function class (modulo an \(f(x)\) baseline) consistent with Bradley–Terry/Plackett–Luce can be represented as \(r(x,y)=\beta\log\tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) for some \(\pi\). What are the precise assumptions? For example, do we require (1) \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)>0\) on the support of the optimal policy, (2) a finite action space (finite set of sequences) or at least countable support, and (3) measurability or boundedness of \(r\)? Also, does the result depend on the reward being only identifiable up to an additive \(f(x)\) term?

questions.title: How do reward equivalence classes \(r(x,y)\sim r'(x,y)+f(x)\) affect identifiability and the induced optimal policy?
questions.question_body: The paper defines an equivalence relation on rewards that differ by an \(x\)-only term \(f(x)\), and states that (i) Bradley–Terry/Plackett–Luce preferences are invariant to this and (ii) the KL-constrained optimal policy is also invariant. Could someone give a concrete example illustrating why adding \(f(x)\) leaves the optimal policy \(\pi_r\) unchanged? Also, how does this under-specification relate to practical issues like reward normalization used in RLHF (e.g., zero-mean rewards)?

questions.title: How does DPO generalize to k-way Plackett–Luce rankings, and what is the resulting loss?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that the derivation extends to Plackett–Luce models when we have ranked lists, not just pairs. What is the explicit DPO loss when the data provide a total order \(y_{(1)}\succ y_{(2)}\succ\dots\succ y_{(k)}\) under the Plackett–Luce assumption? Is it the negative log-likelihood of a cascade of softmaxes over the policy-to-reference log-ratios, i.e., terms like \(\log\tfrac{\exp(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_{(j)}\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{(j)}\mid x)})}{\sum_{m\ge j}\exp(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_{(m)}\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_{(m)}\mid x)})}\)? Any computational or stability differences compared to the pairwise case?

questions.title: What happens if \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) is chosen to be uniform—does DPO reduce to standard logistic regression on log-likelihoods?
questions.question_body: Suppose I take \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\) to be uniform over a fixed finite candidate set for each \(x\). Then the DPO objective reduces to a logistic loss on \(\beta\log\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\) differences. Is this interpretation correct? If so, does using a uniform reference make DPO more prone to over-optimization or distribution shift, since the implicit reward \(\hat r_\theta=\beta\log\pi_\theta\) has no baseline anchor to the original model? Are there reasons to avoid a uniform reference in practice, especially with open-ended language generation where the candidate set is huge?

questions.title: How is the KL between \(\pi\) and \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) computed and controlled in DPO experiments, given DPO has no explicit KL penalty?
questions.question_body: In the experiments, the paper reports a sequence-level KL between \(\pi\) and \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) and shows a reward–KL frontier. Since the DPO loss does not include an explicit KL penalty, how is the realized KL controlled—only via the choice of \(\beta\)? Is the KL measured as a sum of per-token KLs over sampled sequences from \(\pi\), or evaluated on a fixed set of prompts with teacher-forced targets? Is there a principled way to select \(\beta\) to achieve a desired KL without sweeping?

questions.title: Can you give a simple example showing why unlikelihood training can cause degeneration while DPO does not?
questions.question_body: The paper cautions that a naive objective that increases \(\log\pi(y_w\mid x)\) and decreases \(\log\pi(y_l\mid x)\) (unlikelihood) can lead to degeneration, while DPO’s weighting avoids this. Could someone provide a minimal illustrative example (e.g., a toy vocabulary with two or three tokens) showing how unlikelihood can push the model toward pathological solutions (such as always outputting very short answers or collapsing modes), and how the DPO logistic weighting prevents that by downweighting already-correctly-ordered pairs?

questions.title: Is there a principled relationship between DPO’s \(\beta\) and the inference-time sampling temperature?
questions.question_body: Both \(\beta\) in DPO and temperature at inference rescale logits in different places: \(\beta\) scales the implicit reward/log-ratio during training, while sampling temperature rescales the model logits at decode time. Is there any theoretical relationship between these two scalings? For example, if \(\beta\) is set too low or too high, can an appropriate choice of sampling temperature compensate at inference, or do they affect qualitatively different trade-offs (e.g., preference alignment vs. diversity)?

questions.title: How exactly does the control-as-inference view lead to the objective with the normalization term in Eq. (14)?
questions.question_body: The paper rewrites the RLHF optimization as minimizing \(\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\Vert\pi^*(\cdot\mid x)]\), which expands to an expectation of \(f(r_\phi,\pi_{\text{ref}},\beta)-\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\), where \(f\) contains a \(-\beta\log\sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(r_\phi/\beta)\) term. Could someone derive this decomposition in detail and explain the interpretation of this term as a soft value (or partition function) baseline? How does dropping or misestimating this term increase variance in actor–critic training, and why does the DPO reparameterization circumvent the need to estimate it?

questions.title: Can DPO be adapted to token-level or step-wise preferences instead of sequence-level pairs?
questions.question_body: DPO is presented for sequence-level preferences between completions \(y_w\) and \(y_l\). If I have feedback at the token level or at intermediate steps (e.g., a human marks certain tokens or spans as better), can the DPO derivation be adapted to operate on partial sequences \(y_{1:t}\)? Would the loss become a sum over steps of Bradley–Terry terms using \(\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_t\mid x, y_{<t})}\), or are there pitfalls due to the BT model assuming comparisons at the same "granularity"?

questions.title: Under what conditions is DPO’s MLE consistent with the true preference distribution (as cited to Bong 2022)?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that, as a reparameterized Bradley–Terry model, DPO enjoys consistency under suitable assumptions (citing Bong 2022). What are the exact conditions for consistency here? For example, do we require independent and identically distributed pairwise comparisons for each \(x\), sufficient coverage of the response space, and a correctly specified link function (logistic)? How does function approximation error from using a neural \(\pi_\theta\) instead of a linear model affect consistency claims?

questions.title: What if \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)=0\) for a logged sample—how are the log-ratios and gradients defined in DPO?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss uses \(\log\tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\). If the logged dataset includes a completion \(y\) such that \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)=0\) (e.g., due to truncation, tokenization issues, or a reference model with limited support), the log-ratio is undefined. What assumptions or safeguards ensure this cannot happen (e.g., \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) must have full support on the logged pairs)? In practice, is smoothing or adding a small \(\epsilon\) to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) used, and how would that affect the theoretical equivalence to the KL-constrained objective?

questions.title: Without on-policy sampling, how does DPO avoid overfitting to a fixed set of pairs and discover better responses?
questions.question_body: Since DPO trains on an offline fixed dataset of preference pairs, how does it avoid overfitting to those particular responses and missing higher-quality responses that were never shown? Is the idea that reweighting log-ratios relative to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) coupled with generalization of \(\pi_\theta\) suffices, similar to supervised fine-tuning? In what settings might we need online data collection or self-play (e.g., generating new candidate pairs from the current \(\pi_\theta\)) to keep improving, and can DPO be used in such a loop without abandoning its simplicity?

questions.title: How are EOS and variable-length completions handled when computing \(\log \pi(y\mid x)\) for DPO?
questions.question_body: When computing sequence log-likelihoods for \(y_w\) and \(y_l\), do we include the EOS token probability as part of \(\pi(y\mid x)\)? If \(y_w\) and \(y_l\) have different lengths, is there any normalization or padding strategy, or does DPO simply sum the log-probabilities over the exact tokenization of each completion? Could differences in EOS handling systematically bias the preference loss (e.g., preferring shorter sequences due to fewer EOS penalties)?
